Metallic bonding and the properties of metals 
Metals occupy the left-hand side of the pericdic table. In the solid state, 
atoms of metals lose one or more outer electrons and form a lattice of metal 
cations surrounded by a“sea” of delocalized electrons. The electrostatic 
attraction between these cations and the delocalized electrons is known as 
metallic bonding.

Metals conduct electricity because their delocalized electrons can move freely 
in the solid or liquid states and so act as electric charge carriers. 
Metals conduct heat because the delocalized valence electrons are free to 
move and transfer thermal energy rapidly from one part of the metal to another. 
Metals are malleable because there are no directional bonds to be broken; the 
cations can slide past one another when a force is applied (figure 15). 
Strength of metallic bonding 
The strength of metallic bonding depends on three factors: the number of 
valence electrons that can be delocalized, the charge on the metal cation and 
the ionic radius. Across periods, both the number of valence electrons and the 
ionic charge increase, so the strength of metallic bonding and thus the melting 
points also increase. Down a group, the melting points of main group metals 
decrease because of the increasing ionic radii, as larger cations experience 
weaker electrostatic attraction to the delocalized electrons. 
with other metals or non-metals; this is discussed in Structure 2.4. 
Alloys often have greater mechanical strength than their individual 
components because ions of different sizes form a less regular lattice in 
which it is more difficult for the cations to slide past one another. Alloys 
may also have greater resistance to corrosion than pure metals. 
Example 13 
Explain the difference in the melting points of potassium and calcium. 
Metal Melting point / °C 
potassium (K) 63.4 
calcium (Ca) 842 
Solution 
The melting point of a metal depends on the strength of the electrostatic 
forces of attraction that hold the cations within the “sea” of delocalized 
electrons. The melting point of calcium is greater than the melting point of 
potassium because: 
* calcium has two delocalized electrons per atom, whereas potassium 
has only one; this means that the electrostatic attraction between the 
cations and the delocalized electrons is greater in calcium 
* calcium forms a 2+ ion whereas potassium forms a T+ ion, so the 
electrostatic attraction between the cations and the delocalized 
electrons is also greater in calcium 
* theionic radius of K* (138 pm) is larger than the ionic radius of Ca** 
(100 pm), so the delocalized electrons are more strongly attracted to 
the Ca* ion.

substances. The physical properties of a material (melting point, permeability, conductivity, 
elasticity, brittleness) are related to its bonding and structure. 
A chemical bond can be considered as the “glue” that holds atoms together 
in molecules (covalent or polar covalent bonding), in ionic compounds 
(ionic bonding) and in metals (metallic bonding). Chemical bonding is best 
described as a continuum between all three models. With the exception of 
pure covalent or pure metallic bonding in some elementary substances, most 
chemical bonds have mixed character. For example, polar covalent bonds 
are intermediate between covalent and ionic (table 11) while bonding in 
metalloids is intermediate between metallic and covalent.

B
Magnesium has more delocalized electrons per atom (two instead of one), higher ionic charge (2+ instead of 1+) and smaller ionic radius (72 pm instead of 102 pm) than sodium. All three factors increase the strength of metallic bonding and thus the melting point of magnesium as compared with sodium.
